title: Cyclotomic Hecke and Quiver Hecke Algebras

items.title: Arbitrary-level cyclotomic Hecke, Murphy cell and multipartition Schur modules
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge0$ and $\ell\ge1$, and let $z,U_1,\dots,U_\ell$
be units of $R$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). The **arbitrary-level
cyclotomic Hecke algebra** $H_n=H_n(R;z;U_1,\dots,U_\ell)$ is the $R$-algebra
presented by invertible commuting elements $X_1,\dots,X_n$ and generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ subject to the relations
$$(T_i-z)(T_i+1)=0,\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1},\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(|i-j|>1),$$
$$T_iX_iT_i=zX_{i+1},\qquad X_jT_i=T_iX_j\quad(j\notin\{i,i+1\}),\qquad \prod_{a=1}^{\ell}(X_1-U_a)=0 .$$
For $n=0$ set $H_0=R$. The **grading variable** of this page is $v$, not the
unit $z$: the two are identified only where a statement says so explicitly.

**Multipartitions and Murphy data.** An $\ell$-**multipartition** of $n$ is an
ordered tuple $\lambda=(\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(\ell)})$ of partitions
with $\sum_{b}|\lambda^{(b)}|=n$ ([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]).
Multipartitions are partially ordered by dominance, $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ meaning
that $\sum_{b<k}|\lambda^{(b)}|+\sum_{j\le m}\lambda^{(k)}_j\ge
\sum_{b<k}|\mu^{(b)}|+\sum_{j\le m}\mu^{(k)}_j$ for all $k,m$. Fill the
diagram $t^\lambda$ with $1,\dots,n$ in component order, then row order, then
column order. Put $a_k:=\sum_{b<k}|\lambda^{(b)}|$,
$u_\lambda:=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell}\prod_{j\le a_k}(X_j-U_k)$,
$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w$, and $m_\lambda:=x_\lambda u_\lambda$,
where $S_\lambda$ is the row subgroup: the subgroup of $S_n$ stabilizing the
rows of $t^\lambda$
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $M_\lambda:=m_\lambda H_n$ for
the right $H_n$-submodule generated by $m_\lambda$
([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). The **presentation involution** $*$ of $H_n$
fixes every $X_j$ and every $T_i$ and reverses products. For standard
tableaux $s,t$ of shape $\lambda$ put $m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$,
where the right tableau action is $t\cdot w:=w^{-1}\cdot t$ (the left action relabels entries), and $d(s)$ is determined by $t^\lambda\cdot d(s)=s$.
Denote by $H^{>\lambda}$ the span of the higher Murphy shapes once their
basis and cell law is established by
[[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]], and by
$S_\lambda$ the right cell (**Specht**) module with basis $m_t$ and the
action given by that cell law; its cellular form defines
$D_\lambda:=S_\lambda/\operatorname{rad}S_\lambda$, which may vanish.

**Types.** The types used below are **exactly** all $\ell$-multipartitions of
$n$, including tuples with empty components — not all multicompositions. A
**semistandard tableau** $S$ has entries the labels $(i,k)$ (row $i$ in
component $k$) ordered by component first and then by row, weakly increasing
along rows, strictly increasing down columns, and a label of component $a$
may occur only in physical component $b\le a$
([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]); the **type** of $S$ is the
multipartition counting each label with the multiplicity of the corresponding
row. For standard $s$ let $\mu(s)$ be the tableau obtained from $s$ by
replacing each entry by its row-and-component in $t^{\mu}$. Put
$$m_{(S,t)}:=\sum_{s:\,\mu(s)=S}m_{st},\qquad m_{(S,T)}:=\sum_{s,t:\,\mu(s)=S,\ \nu(t)=T}m_{st}.$$
Let
$$M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda\ \text{multipartition of}\ n}M_\lambda,\qquad C_n:=\operatorname{End}_{H_n}(M),$$
with ordinary composition ([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]). For
$S,T$ of shape $\lambda$ and types $\mu,\nu$, the map $\varphi_{ST}$ — once
justified by [[lem-cyclotomic-semistandard-sums-give-schur-endomorphism-basis]] —
sends $m_\alpha h$ to $\delta_{\alpha,\nu}m_{(S,T)}h$. Its right cell module
$\Delta_\lambda$ has basis $v_T$ over the semistandard $T$ of multipartition
types, with contravariant cell form and quotient $L_\lambda$. Let $T^\lambda$
be the unique tableau of shape and type $\lambda$, and let $e_\lambda$ be the
identity projection onto $M_\lambda$. Put $\omega:=(\varnothing,\dots,\varnothing,(1^n))$
and $e:=e_\omega$; then $m_\omega=1$, so $M_\omega=H_n$, and $H_n$ is an
actual direct summand of $M$. The weight projections used by the Jantzen
theory below are the $e_\nu$ with $\nu$ a multipartition. Write
$K_{(\lambda,\nu)}:=\#\operatorname{SStd}_\nu(\lambda)$ for the number of
semistandard tableaux of shape $\lambda$ and type $\nu$.

**Boundary of the definition.** All asserted module, form and map laws are
discharged by the linked local suppliers
[[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]],
[[lem-cyclotomic-semistandard-sums-give-schur-endomorphism-basis]] and
[[thm-cyclotomic-schur-standards-and-schur-functor-control-block-linkage]];
the definition itself claims no proof of them and no primitive
residue-content classification. No choice principle is used: only finite
bases, finite subgroup and coset decompositions, finite filtrations and
explicit polynomial identities occur.
items.strategy: Explicit definitions; existence of quotient and finite direct sums is elementary. The asserted cell/module/map well-definedness is supplied by the declared justified_by local results, whose statements refer back to this definition.

items.title: Laurent binomial valuation at one over any field
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, let $F[t,t^{-1}]$ be its Laurent polynomial ring
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]), and let $v_1$ be the $(t-1)$-adic
valuation on the nonzero elements of $F[t,t^{-1}]$: for $0\ne f$,
$$v_1(f):=\max\{n\ge0:(t-1)^n\mid f\ \text{in}\ F[t,t^{-1}]\},$$
so that $v_1(f)=0$ exactly when $f(1)\ne0$
([[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]). Let $A,B\in F\setminus\{0\}$, let $u,v\in\mathbb Z$,
put $N:=u-v$ and $f:=At^u-Bt^v$.

1. If $A\ne B$, then $v_1(f)=0$.
2. If $A=B$ and $N\ne0$, then $v_1(f)=1$ when $\operatorname{char}F=0$, and
   $v_1(f)=p^{v_p(|N|)}$ when $\operatorname{char}F=p>0$; here $v_p$ is the
   exponent of $p$ in $|N|$, i.e. $N=p^r m$ with $p\nmid m$
   ([[def-ring-characteristic]]).
3. If $A=B$ and $N=0$, then $f=0$, and the zero element has no finite valuation.

In the intended application the Laurent polynomials $Q_aq_H^{\,j-i}t^{\,na+j-i}$
(foot residues of the Jantzen expression) are compared by this lemma: it
computes their valuation exactly when their difference is nonzero and prevents
replacing valuations by an equality-of-residues indicator in positive
characteristic.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.







**Given:** The field $F$, the Laurent polynomial ring $F[t,t^{-1}]$ with unit $t$, the valuation $v_1$ of the Statement, and the data of [F1]–[F3].







1.1 Reduction to $N$ and to $A/B$. Since $Bt^v$ is a unit of $F[t,t^{-1}]$ with inverse $B^{-1}t^{-v}$ by [F1], the identity $At^u-Bt^v=Bt^v\bigl((A/B)t^N-1\bigr)$ and [F2] give $v_1(At^u-Bt^v)=v_1\bigl((A/B)t^N-1\bigr)$; moreover if $N<0$ then $t^{N}-1=-t^{N}(t^{-N}-1)$ with $-t^{N}$ a unit, so $v_1(t^{N}-1)=v_1(t^{|N|}-1)$ by [F1] and [F2]. [F1, F2]

1.2 The case $A=B$, $N=0$. Then $f=At^u-Bt^v=At^u-At^u=0$ by [F1], the zero element of $F[t,t^{-1}]$; since $(t-1)^n\mid0$ for every $n$, the set in the definition of $v_1$ is unbounded and no finite value is assigned. [F1]

2.1 The case $A\ne B$. Evaluating the Laurent polynomial $(A/B)t^N-1$ at $t=1$ gives $A/B-1\ne0$, so the factor $t-1$ cannot divide $(A/B)t^N-1$: a product containing $t-1$ would evaluate to $0$ under the ring homomorphism $f\mapsto f(1)$ with $1\mapsto1$. Hence $v_1((A/B)t^N-1)=0$ by [F2], and the reduction of step 1.1 gives $v_1(f)=0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

2.2 The case $A=B$, $\operatorname{char}F=0$, $N\ne0$. Here $f=A(t^u-t^v)=At^v(t^N-1)$ with $At^v$ a unit, so by step 1.1 the valuation equals $v_1(t^{|N|}-1)$, while $t^{|N|}-1=(t-1)(1+t+\cdots+t^{|N|-1})$ with second factor evaluating at $t=1$ to $|N|\cdot1_F\ne0$ by [F3] and therefore of valuation $0$ by [F2]; the valuation is additive on this factorisation of the nonzero polynomial $t^{|N|}-1$, so $v_1(f)=1$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The case $A=B$, $\operatorname{char}F=p>0$, $N\ne0$. Write $|N|=p^rm$ with $r\ge0$ and $p\nmid m$. In characteristic $p$ the identity $(x-1)^{p^r}=x^{p^r}-1$ follows by iterating $(x-1)^p=x^p-1$ (the intermediate binomial coefficients $\binom{p}{i}$, $1\le i\le p-1$, are multiples of $p$); applying it to $x=t^m$ gives $t^{|N|}-1=(t^m-1)^{p^r}=(t-1)^{p^r}(1+t+\cdots+t^{m-1})^{p^r}$. The second factor evaluates at $t=1$ to $m^{p^r}\cdot1_F$, which is nonzero because $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ by [F3]; it thus has valuation $0$ by [F2], so $v_1(t^{|N|}-1)=p^r$, and step 1.1 gives $v_1(f)=p^r=p^{v_p(|N|)}$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Ultra-tight multisets admit integer column potentials
items.statement:
Let $r\ge1$ and $L_r:=\mathbb Z^r/\mathbb Z(1,\dots,1)$
([[def-free-abelian-group]], [[def-integers]]). For a finite multiset $X$ of
elements of $L_r$ ([[def-multiset-and-powerset-constructions]]), call $X$
**tight** if
$$(x_k-x_l)-(y_k-y_l)\le2$$
for all occurrences $x,y\in X$ and all indices $k,l\in\{1,\dots,r\}$. A
**zero exchange** replaces two occurrences $x,y$ by $x-e_k+e_l$ and
$y+e_k-e_l$ whenever $(x_k-x_l)-(y_k-y_l)=2$; this relation is symmetric.
Call $X$ **ultra-tight** if every finite zero-exchange sequence starting at
$X$ ends in a tight multiset. Then $X$ is ultra-tight if and only if there is
some $s\in\mathbb Z^r$ with
$$x_k-x_l\le s_k-s_l+1\qquad\text{for every }x\in X\ \text{and every }k,l .$$
This includes the empty multiset and $r=1$.
items.strategy:
For the empty multiset take s=0. For nonempty X the complete finite induction follows.

Work in L_r=Z^r/Z(1,…,1). A finite multiset X is tight if

(x_k−x_l)−(y_k−y_l)≤2 for every x,y∈X and every k,l.

A zero exchange replaces x,y by x−e_k+e_l and y+e_k−e_l when the displayed difference equals 2. This relation is symmetric; call X ultra-tight if every multiset obtainable by finitely many zero exchanges is tight. These notions do not depend on representatives in Z^r.

**Lemma.** X is ultra-tight iff there are integers s₁,…,s_r such that x_k−x_l≤s_k−s_l+1 for every x∈X and every k,l.

The reverse implication has a short direct proof. After replacing x by x−s, every row has maximum minus minimum at most one. A zero exchange must have x_k−x_l=1 and y_k−y_l=−1, so it merely swaps the high and low values in these two coordinates of each row. The row spread remains at most one. The property is preserved by every zero exchange and implies tightness.

Here is a full proof of the forward implication, adapted from the actual proof of Fayers Proposition 2.2 and its induction step Proposition 2.3 (author PDF pp.11–15). We induct on r. The r=1 case is trivial. Projection forgetting the last coordinate takes an ultra-tight multiset to one in L_(r−1): every zero exchange in the projection lifts using the same pair of coordinate indices and the same labeled multiset occurrences. Hence the induction hypothesis supplies potentials for the first r−1 coordinates. It remains to extend them to coordinate r, preserving all previous bounds.

Write a_kl=s_k−s_l. Suppose bounds |(x_k−x_l)−a_kl|≤1 are known whenever k,l≤r−1 or k,l≥t+1, with 1≤t≤r−1. We show how to obtain such bounds also for k,l≥t. For t=r−1, tightness says the integer differences x_(r−1)−x_r have range at most two, so choose their integer midpoint for s_(r−1)−s_r; the potentials on the first r−1 coordinates stay fixed.

For t<r−1, if the current potentials already bound x_t−x_r, nothing is needed. Otherwise, after replacing every row x and every potential s by its negative if necessary, choose x∈X with x_t−x_r≥a_tr+2. For t<u<r, the old bounds imply x_t−x_u≤a_tu+1 and x_u−x_r≤a_ur+1. Thus x_t−x_r=a_tr+2, and both inequalities are equalities for every u. Tightness implies, for every y∈X,

a_tr≤y_t−y_r≤a_tr+2.

Form a directed graph on {1,…,r}, with an edge k→l when some y∈X has y_k−y_l=a_kl−1.

If no path leads from t to r, let T be the vertices reachable from t and let R be the complement. Change potentials to s'_k=s_k+1 for k∈T and s'_k=s_k for k∈R. Then a'_tr=a_tr+1, giving the new (t,r) bound. Any other previously controlled difference with a'_kl≥a_kl retains its upper bound. If a'_kl=a_kl−1, then k∈R,l∈T. The reverse pair has no edge T→R, so its old lower bound y_l−y_k≥a_lk−1 improves to ≥a_lk; hence y_k−y_l≤a_kl=a'_kl+1. Apply this to ordered pairs and their reverses. All required bounds hold.

If a path does lead from t to r, choose a shortest path t=k₁→k₂→⋯→k_h=r and labeled occurrences y₁,…,y_(h−1) witnessing its edges. Its vertices are distinct. Write z=y−s for each witness. On the first r−1 coordinates every such z has spread at most one, by the old bounds. Therefore one occurrence cannot witness two edges both ending before r: their low-to-high values would give the shortcut k_m→k_(n+1) for m<n. Nor can it witness an earlier edge and the last edge: a last-edge witness has z_(k_(h−1))=z_r−1; tightness against the chosen x gives z_k−z_r≥−1 for every k<r, while spread at most one on the first r−1 coordinates gives z_k−z_r≤0. An earlier edge witnessed by the same row would thus start at z_r−1, giving a shortcut from its starting vertex directly to r. Hence all edge witnesses are distinct occurrences.

For each k<r, x_k−x_r≥a_kr+1: for k≥t this was proved above, and for k<t use x_k−x_t≥a_kt−1 and x_t−x_r=a_tr+2. Put x^(m)=x−e_(k_(m+1))+e_r for 1≤m<h. At m=h−1 this is x itself. We first note why none of the edge witnesses can be the chosen occurrence x. If y_p=x, choose such a p (at most one, since edge witnesses are distinct). It cannot be the last witness, since its edge to r would have x_(k_(h−1))−x_r=a_(k_(h−1),r)−1, contradicting the preceding lower bound. Run the following downward exchange induction using only witnesses with index >p, all distinct from x and from each other. It yields x_(k_(p+1))−x_r=a_(k_(p+1),r)+1. Combining this with x_(k_p)−x_r≥a_(k_p,r)+1 gives x_(k_p)−x_(k_(p+1))≥a_(k_p,k_(p+1)), incompatible with y_p=x witnessing the value a_(k_p,k_(p+1))−1. Thus no witness equals x. This use of the induction is valid on the shorter tail because it needs only its current distinguished row and the tail witnesses, whose occurrences survive all earlier tail exchanges.

Here is that downward induction in full. We prove that some multiset equivalent to X contains x^(m) and the unchanged witnesses y₁,…,y_m, and that x_(k_m)−x_r=a_(k_m,r)+1. The base uses the original X: tightness between x and y_(h−1) says their (k_(h−1),r) differences, which differ by at least two, differ by exactly two, forcing the claimed equality and giving a permitted zero exchange for the next stage. For the induction step, perform the zero exchange between x^(m+1) and y_(m+1) in coordinates k_(m+1),k_(m+2). It creates x^(m) and leaves all earlier witnesses unchanged because their occurrences are distinct. For m≤h−2 neither k_m nor k_(m+1) is r. The already proved equality at k_(m+1), and the lower bound at k_m, give

x^(m)_(k_m)−x^(m)_(k_(m+1)) ≥ a_(k_m,k_(m+1))+1 = (y_m,_(k_m)−y_m,_(k_(m+1)))+2.

The resulting multiset is tight by ultra-tightness. Therefore equality holds, supplying the next zero exchange and forcing x_(k_m)−x_r=a_(k_m,r)+1. This completes the induction.
At m=1 the conclusion is x_t−x_r=a_tr+1, contradicting x_t−x_r=a_tr+2. Therefore an ultra-tight multiset cannot fall in this second case.

This extends the bounds at each t=r−1,r−2,…,1. The r induction proves the lemma. The proof uses only finite multisets and integer arithmetic.

items.title: Affine type-A presentations and charged cyclotomic quotients
items.statement: Let A be a commutative base ring and z a unit. The nondegenerate AFFINE presentation has commuting units X_r and finite generators T_r with T_r²=(z−1)T_r+z, braid/distant relations, T_rX_rT_r=zX_(r+1) and T_rX_s=X_sT_r for s not r,r+1. The degenerate AFFINE presentation over A has commuting x_r and symmetric-group generators s_r, with s_r x_r=x_(r+1)s_r−1, s_r x_(r+1)=x_r s_r+1 and distant mixed commutation. Auxiliary cyclotomic quotients impose a monic polynomial f of degree ℓ only on the first polynomial generator, with unit constant term in NG. Rank zero is A; degree-zero f=1 at positive rank gives zero. For the charged CYCLIC specialization take A=F a field, z=q_H of finite quantum characteristic e>=2, I=Z/eZ an integer LABEL set, λ_i>=0 and ℓ=Σ_iλ_i (a dominant cyclic type-A weight). If q_H!=1 use NG and c_i=q_H^i; if q_H=1 (charF=e) use DG and c_i=i·1_F. Impose f(z_1)=∏_i(z_1−c_i)^{λ_i} to define H^Λ_d. This charged finite-e branch is the native24 scope; the arbitrary-base affine/monic definitions supply its necessary universal PBW/trace proof inputs. No basis, spectrum, primitive blocks or BK isomorphism is asserted by this pure definition. The grading variable v is independent of q_H.
items.strategy: Explicit generators/relations and the quotient ideal define these algebras. The distinct NG values follow from multiplicative order e, while DG integers are distinct because e=charF; no embedding Z/eZ→F is claimed in NG. The source/KLR grading variable v is independent of q_H.

items.title: DVR cellular Jantzen filtration and exact Gram valuation
items.statement:
Let $O$ be a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$ and residue field
$F=O/\pi O$ ([[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]), and let $\nu_\pi$ denote its
valuation. Let $M$ be a finite free $O$-module with an $O$-valued bilinear
pairing $b$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]) whose scalar extension to
$\operatorname{Frac}(O)$ is nondegenerate. For $s\ge0$ put
$$M(s):=\{x\in M:b(x,M)\subseteq\pi^sO\},\qquad M_F^s:=(M(s)+\pi M)/\pi M .$$
Then:

1. $M_F^0=M/\pi M$ and $M_F^1=\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$, where $b_F$ is the
   reduced pairing on $M_F$;
2. the filtration terminates ($M_F^s=0$ for all sufficiently large $s$), and
   for any Gram matrix $G$ of $b$ one has the exact identity
   $$\sum_{s>0}\dim_FM_F^s=\nu_\pi(\det G);$$
3. if an $O$-algebra $A$ acts on $M$ with an anti-involution $*$ satisfying
   $b(ax,y)=b(x,a^*y)$ for all $a\in A$, $x,y\in M$, then every $M(s)$, and
   hence every $M_F^s$, is an $A$-submodule;
4. if $M_F$ is a cellular standard module and $b_F$ is its nonzero cellular form
   ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]), then
   $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$ is its unique maximal submodule and therefore
   coincides with its module radical
   ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]).

The Smith reduction used in the proof works over $O$ without any
characteristic restriction, in particular in characteristic $2$; it uses
independent bases of $M$ and of $M^*=\operatorname{Hom}_O(M,O)$, never a
diagonalization of a symmetric form.
items.strategy:
**Statement.** Let O be a DVR with uniformizer pi and residue field F. Let M be a finite free O-module with an O-valued bilinear pairing b whose scalar extension to Frac(O) is nondegenerate. Set M(s)={x:b(x,M) subset pi^s O} and M_F^s=(M(s)+pi M)/pi M. Then M_F^0=M/pi M, M_F^1=rad(b_F), the filtration terminates, and sum_{s>0}dim_F M_F^s=nu_pi(det G) for any Gram matrix G. If A acts on M with anti-involution * and b(ax,y)=b(x,a* y), all M(s), and hence M_F^s, are submodules. If M_F is a cellular standard module with nonzero cellular form, rad(b_F) is its unique maximal submodule and therefore its module radical.

**Proof.** View the form as an O-linear map phi:M -> M*=Hom_O(M,O), x -> b(x,-). Its determinant is nonzero, so it has full rank. A direct Smith reduction needs no characteristic restriction: choose a nonzero matrix entry of least valuation, move it to the upper-left corner, and multiply its row by a unit to make it pi^a. Every entry is divisible by pi^a. Row and column subtraction eliminate its column and row, leaving a smaller matrix over O. Iterate. Since all elimination coefficients belong to O and every operation is invertible over O, this gives independent bases of M and M* in which phi sends u_j to pi^{a_j}v_j, with all a_j>=0. Thus

$$M(s)=\bigoplus_j\pi^{\max(0,s-a_j)}O u_j,\qquad \dim_F M_F^s=\#\{j:a_j\ge s\}.$$

Consequently M_F^s=0 for s>max_j a_j and sum_{s>0}dim M_F^s=sum_j a_j=nu_pi(det G). Reduction mod pi shows directly that M(1)/its reduction consists of exactly the vectors orthogonal to every vector of M_F, proving M_F^1=rad(b_F). Contravariance gives b(ax,y)=b(x,a*y) in pi^s O whenever x in M(s), proving stability.

For the last assertion use the defining cellular multiplication, not merely the word cellularity: in the standard module, for every basis label u and label v the corresponding cell element acts as w -> b_F(v,w)u (with left/right conventions transposed if necessary). If a submodule N contains w outside rad(b_F), choose v with b_F(v,w) !=0. Every basis vector u belongs to N by this rank-one action, so N=M_F. Therefore every proper submodule is contained in rad(b_F). The radical itself is proper because the form is nonzero, and the same argument shows the quotient is simple. It is the unique maximal submodule and equals the module radical. This completes the proof, including characteristic 2: the Smith reduction uses different domain and codomain bases, never diagonalization of a symmetric form.

items.title: Universal nondegenerate affine Hecke ordered monomials form a basis
items.statement:
Let $R:=\mathbb Z[z^{\pm1},U_1^{\pm1},\dots,U_\ell^{\pm1}]$ be the universal
Laurent parameter ring of
[[def-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-cell-and-schur-modules]], and let
$H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$ be the $R$-algebra presented there by the commuting units
$X_1,\dots,X_n$, the generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the quadratic, braid,
distant, Bernstein and mixed-commutation relations — **without** imposing the
first-variable cyclotomic relation. Then:

1. both families
   $$X^aT_w\quad\text{and}\quad T_wX^a\qquad(a\in\mathbb Z^n,\ w\in S_n)$$
   are $R$-bases of $H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$, and the same two families are bases
   after arbitrary base change to a commutative ring in which $z$ is a unit;
2. left multiplication by any nonzero element of the Laurent polynomial
   subalgebra $R[X_1^{\pm1},\dots,X_n^{\pm1}]\subseteq H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$ is
   injective;
3. after localizing at the differences $X_i-X_j$ ($i\ne j$), the algebra maps
   into the rational crossed product of the fraction field of the polynomial
   ring with $S_n$, and in that localization the elements
   $$\Phi_i:=T_i-\frac{(z-1)X_{i+1}}{X_{i+1}-X_i} =T_i-c_{i,i+1},\qquad c_{ij}:=\frac{(z-1)X_j}{X_j-X_i},$$
   satisfy $\Phi_if=s_i(f)\Phi_i$ for every (localized) Laurent polynomial $f$.

No cyclotomic basis, Brundan–Kleshchev theorem, trace form or
primitive-content assertion is used.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The universal domain $R$, its Laurent polynomial ring $P=R[X_1^{\pm1},\dots,X_n^{\pm1}]$, the fraction field $K=\operatorname{Frac}(P)$, and the data of [F1]–[F3].

1.1 Ordered spanning without localization. For every $f\in P$ the presentation relations give $T_if=s_i(f)T_i+c_{i,i+1}(f-s_i(f))$, where $c_{i,i+1}=(z-1)X_{i+1}/(X_{i+1}-X_i)$. The correction is in $P$: $f-s_i(f)$ is divisible by $X_{i+1}-X_i$, first for ordinary monomials by the difference-of-powers identity, and then for Laurent monomials after multiplying by a symmetric Laurent monomial unit. For $f=X_i$ this is the Bernstein relation, for $f=X_{i+1}$ it is its conjugate using the quadratic relation, and the general formula follows by addition and the product rule $f g-s_i(f g)=(f-s_i(f))g+s_i(f)(g-s_i(g))$, including inverse generators by applying that rule to $f f^{-1}=1$. Moving a polynomial across a $T$ reduces the number of misplaced polynomial factors, and correction terms reduce the number of $T$ factors; the finite Hecke relations then span the remaining words by $T_w$. Thus $H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$ is spanned over $P$ by the $T_w$, and the presentation anti-involution fixing $X_i,T_i$ gives right ordered spanning too. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 A representation of the unlocalized presentation. Form $K\rtimes S_n$ with multiplication $(f\sigma)(g\tau)=f\sigma(g)\sigma\tau$. For distinct indices set $c_{ij}=(z-1)X_j/(X_j-X_i)$ and $d_{ij}=(X_j-zX_i)/(X_j-X_i)=z-c_{ij}$, and assign $T_i\mapsto c_{i,i+1}+d_{i,i+1}s_i$, $X_j\mapsto X_j$. The rational identities $c_{ij}+c_{ji}=z-1$ and $d_{ij}d_{ji}=z+(z-1)c_{ij}-c_{ij}^2$ give the quadratic relation. For three distinct indices, expansion of the two braid products in their six permutation coefficients agrees: the longest coefficients are $d_{ij}d_{ik}d_{jk}$ in either order; the two length-two coefficients agree by commuting scalar factors; the length-one and identity coefficients agree using $c_{ij}c_{jk}=c_{ik}(c_{ij}+c_{jk}-(z-1))$ together with the preceding quadratic identities. These identities follow by multiplying by the common product of the differences and expanding the polynomial numerators. Distant relations follow from disjoint variable pairs. Finally $T_if-s_i(f)T_i=c_{i,i+1}(f-s_i(f))$, so the Bernstein and mixed relations hold. All denominators here are nonzero polynomials in independent variables in the domain $P$. This defines a homomorphism from the unlocalized presented algebra to $K\rtimes S_n$. [F1, algebra]

1.3 Independence over the base ring. For a reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, the coefficient of the group element $w$ in the image of $T_w$ is
$$D_w=d_{i_1,i_1+1}\,s_{i_1}(d_{i_2,i_2+1})\cdots(s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_{k-1}})(d_{i_k,i_k+1})\ne0.$$
Every factor is a nonzero rational function; every other term uses a proper subword and therefore represents a permutation of length less than $k$ by [F3]. In a finite relation $\sum_w f_wT_w=0$ with $f_w\in P$, select a label $w$ of maximal length with $f_w\ne0$. Its group-element coefficient is $f_wD_w$ and receives no contribution from any other label of that maximal length or from shorter labels, so it is nonzero in $K$, a contradiction. Hence the $T_w$ are $P$-linearly independent and the representation is injective. Since the Laurent monomials $X^a$ are an $R$-basis of $P$, this proves that $X^aT_w$ are an $R$-basis; the anti-involution proves the right basis. Tensoring this free basis with any commutative $R$-algebra preserves it, and tensoring the generators-and-relations presentation gives exactly the same affine presentation over that algebra. As the unused $U$ parameters do not enter the relations, any commutative coefficient ring with unit $z$ is obtained by sending every $U_a$ to $1$. Thus the asserted arbitrary base change is valid, without inverting differences in the base-changed algebra. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.1 Localization and intertwiners. Let $S$ be the multiplicative set generated by all $X_i-X_j$ with $i\ne j$. It is invariant under $S_n$. The mixed formula of step 1.1 extends to $S^{-1}P$ by the same product rule and by solving the formula for inverses of elements of $S$; the correction remains in $S^{-1}P$. Consequently adjoining these inverses gives the algebra with free left coefficient module $\bigoplus_w(S^{-1}P)T_w$ and the same multiplication rules. This realizes the localization: the inverse formulas make it universal among homomorphisms inverting $S$, and its injective representation in $K\rtimes S_n$ follows from the identical maximal-length argument of step 1.3. In it put $\Phi_i=T_i-c_{i,i+1}$; the mixed formula gives $\Phi_if=s_i(f)\Phi_i$ for all $f\in S^{-1}P$. Products $\Phi_w$ along reduced words have unitriangular expansions in the $T_v$, because selecting every $T$ gives $T_w$ and selecting any scalar correction leaves strictly shorter words; thus they too form a basis over $S^{-1}P$. No parameter difference $U_a-U_b$, quantum factorial or Gram determinant is inverted. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

2.2 Polynomial multiplication is injective over the universal domain. If $0\ne f\in P$ and $h=\sum_w f_wT_w$, then $fh=0$ gives $ff_w=0$ for each $w$ by step 1.3. Since $P$ is a domain, every $f_w=0$, so $h=0$. The right-basis argument gives the analogous right multiplication result. This injectivity assertion is over the universal domain, as in Statement (2), and does not assert injectivity of nonzero zero divisors after arbitrary base change. [step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Subword support in the localization. Expanding a reduced product $T_w=\prod_t(\Phi_{i_t}+c_{i_t,i_t+1})$ and moving coefficients left using step 2.1 gives terms supported on products of subwords of the reduced word. Every coefficient is a sum of products of permuted $c$ functions and hence has only variable-difference denominators. Equivalently, in the crossed product $\Phi_i=d_{i,i+1}s_i$, so moving a localized polynomial $f$ through such a term replaces it by the corresponding subword permutation applied to $f$. This proves the subword expansion used by consumers and the asserted intertwining throughout the embedded localization. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Conclusion. Step 1.3 proves both ordered bases over $R$ and after arbitrary base change with unit $z$; step 2.2 proves the universal-domain injectivity; and steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the localized embedding and intertwining identity. For $n=0$ there are no polynomial or Hecke generators, $S_0$ consists of the identity, the lone ordered monomial is $1$, and $H_0^{\mathrm{aff}}=R$; all localization and intertwining clauses are then vacuous. No cyclotomic basis, trace form, primitive-content assertion or Brundan–Kleshchev result is used. [step 1.3, step 2.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Bounded ordered monomials span the cyclotomic Hecke quotients
items.statement:
Over any commutative base ring $A$ with invertible nondegenerate parameter,
use the defining relations of
[[def-type-a-affine-presentations-and-charged-cyclotomic-quotients]], writing
$q_H$ for the nondegenerate Hecke parameter. For a monic cyclotomic polynomial
$f$ of degree $\ell>0$, with unit constant term in the nondegenerate branch,
the quotient by $f(X_1)=0$ is spanned by
$$X_1^{a_1}\cdots X_d^{a_d}T_w,\qquad 0\le a_r<\ell,\ w\in S_d,$$
and the degenerate quotient by $f(x_1)=0$ is spanned by
$$x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_d^{a_d}w,\qquad 0\le a_r<\ell,\ w\in S_d .$$
In particular, over a field $F$ each quotient has dimension at most
$\ell^dd!$. This applies to $f(t)=\prod_{i\in I}(t-q_H^i)^{\lambda_i}$ and
$f(t)=\prod_{i\in I}(t-i)^{\lambda_i}$ in the two finite-quantum-characteristic
branches, with $\ell=\sum_i\lambda_i$. No independence and no separate relation
$f(X_r)=0$ or $f(x_r)=0$ for $r>1$ is asserted. If $\ell=0$ and $d>0$, the
imposed relation $1=0$ gives the zero algebra with empty spanning family; for
$d=0$ the algebra is $A$ with the singleton empty monomial.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The two presentations over $A$, the cyclotomic quotient by

$f(X_1)=0$ (nondegenerate) or $f(x_1)=0$ (degenerate), and the data of

[F1]–[F2].

1.1 Elementary straightening of polynomials past a simple generator. In the nondegenerate branch the mixed relation gives, for a polynomial $p$ in the commuting variables, $T_rp=(s_rp)T_r-(q_H-1)X_{r+1}\frac{p-s_rp}{X_r-X_{r+1}},$ and in the degenerate branch $s_rp=(s_rp)s_r-\frac{p-s_rp}{x_r-x_{r+1}} .$ Both divided differences are polynomials: for $p=X_r^m$ the first identity is $T_rX_r^m=X_{r+1}^mT_r-(q_H-1)(X_r^{m-1}+X_r^{m-2}X_{r+1}+\dots+X_{r+1}^{m-1})X_{r+1}$, which follows from [F1] by induction on $m$, and the second is $s_rx_r^m=x_{r+1}^ms_r-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}x_r^kx_{r+1}^{m-1-k}$, again by induction; the general case follows from the divided-difference product rule for the two variable replacements $X_r\leftrightarrow X_{r+1}$ and $x_r\leftrightarrow x_{r+1}$. Consequently any word in the generators and polynomial variables rewrites as an $A$-linear combination of ordered monomials $X^aT_w$ in the nondegenerate branch (the $T$-word reduced by [F2], polynomial factors collected by commutation) and of $x^aw$ in the degenerate branch. The nondegenerate straightening preserves total polynomial degree; the degenerate one lowers degree by one in the correction term. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The nondegenerate quotient is generated by positive powers. In the nondegenerate branch the relation $f(X_1)=0$ has nonzero constant term $a_0$, so $X_1^{-1}=-a_0^{-1}(X_1^{\ell-1}+a_{\ell-1}X_1^{\ell-2}+\dots+a_1)$ is a polynomial in $X_1$; and from $T_rX_rT_r=q_HX_{r+1}$ one gets $X_{r+1}^{-1}=q_HT_r^{-1}X_r^{-1}T_r^{-1}$ by inverting the equation. Starting from the displayed polynomial expression for $X_1^{-1}$ and iterating this forward recursion expresses every $X_r^{-1}$ through positive powers of $X_1$ and the $T$'s, since $T_r^{-1}=q_H^{-1}(T_r-q_H+1)$ is a polynomial in $T_r$. Therefore the quotient is already generated, as an $A$-module, by words in $X_1,\dots,X_d$ and the $T_r$, and step 1.1 applies to them. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The transported relations in the nondegenerate branch. Put $R_1:=f(X_1)$ and $R_{r+1}:=T_rR_rT_r$; each $R_r$ is zero in the quotient. We claim by induction on $r$ that ordered straightening writes $R_r=q_H^{r-1}X_r^{\ell}+\sum_{a,w}c_{a,w}X_1^{a_1}\cdots X_r^{a_r}T_w,$ where $w\in S_r$, $\sum_ja_j\le\ell$, $a_r<\ell$, and no variable of index above $r$ occurs. The case $r=1$ is the definition, with constant coefficient rearranged. For the induction step, direct summation of the mixed relation gives, for $m\ge1$, $T_rX_r^mT_r=q_HX_{r+1}^m-(q_H-1)\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}X_r^kX_{r+1}^{m-k}T_r,$ and for $m=0$ one uses $T_r^2=(q_H-1)T_r+q_H$. Transporting the leading term $q_H^{r-1}X_r^{\ell}$ therefore produces exactly $q_H^rX_{r+1}^{\ell}$ plus terms of $X_{r+1}$-degree below $\ell$. Each remainder monomial has $X_r$-degree $a_r<\ell$; variables of index below $r$ commute with $T_r$ and with $X_{r+1}$, and $T_w\in H_r$ for $w\in S_r$, so applying the displayed formula to $X_r^{a_r}$ and then straightening the finite words $T_rT_wT_r$, $T_wT_r$ by [F2] produces terms of $X_{r+1}$-degree at most $a_r<\ell$ and total polynomial degree at most $\ell$. This proves the claim. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 The transported relations in the degenerate branch. Put $R_1:=f(x_1)$ and $R_{r+1}:=s_rR_rs_r$. Straightening and induction on $r$ show $R_r=x_r^{\ell}+\sum_{a,w}c_{a,w}x^aw,$ where $w\in S_r$, all occurring variables have index at most $r$, and $\sum_ja_j<\ell$: conjugation transports $x_r^m$ by $s_rx_r^ms_r=x_{r+1}^m-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}x_r^kx_{r+1}^{m-1-k}s_r,$ so the leading term $x_r^{\ell}$ produces $x_{r+1}^{\ell}$ plus correction terms of total degree $\ell-1$, and every old remainder, when straightened, stays of degree below $\ell$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Termination of the nondegenerate reduction. Order exponent vectors lexicographically as $(a_d,a_{d-1},\dots,a_1)$, larger first differing coordinate larger; this is a well-order on $\mathbb N^d$ preserved by addition. Suppose $a_r\ge\ell$ for some $r$ and some spanning monomial $X^aT_w$. Multiplying the zero relation $R_r$ of step 2.2 on the left by $X^{a-\ell e_r}$ and on the right by $T_w$ gives a relation whose leading term is $q_H^{r-1}X^aT_w$ and whose remaining terms all have the same coordinates above $r$ and a strictly smaller $r$-th coordinate (increases in coordinates below $r$ do not affect the lexicographic comparison), with $w\in S_r$ and finite straightening changing no dot exponents. Since $q_H^{r-1}$ is a unit, this solves for $X^aT_w$ as a combination of spanning monomials with strictly smaller exponent vector; well-founded induction on the lexicographic order terminates and expresses every element using only monomials with every $a_r<\ell$. Hence the bounded ordered monomials span the nondegenerate quotient, over $A$ and after any base change. [step 2.2, algebra]

3.2 Termination of the degenerate reduction. If $a_r\ge\ell$, multiply the zero relation $R_r$ of step 2.3 on the left by $x^{a-\ell e_r}$ and on the right by $w$; the leading term is $x^aw$, and every other term has total degree strictly below $\sum_ja_j$ (all other coefficients come from the remainder of $R_r$, of degree $<\ell$). Induction on the total degree $\sum_ja_j$ therefore expresses every element in terms of monomials $x^aw$ with all $a_r<\ell$. This also shows that no relation $f(x_r)=0$ for $r>1$ is claimed: at level one $f(t)=t$, and $x_1=0$ gives $x_2=s_1$, which is exactly the form of the reduced spanning family. [step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 Conclusion. Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 give the spanning statement for the nondegenerate quotient by $f(X_1)=0$, and steps 1.1, 2.3 and 3.2 for the degenerate quotient by $f(x_1)=0$, with all exponents $a_r<\ell$ in both branches and no independence asserted. Since the spanning families have at most $\ell^dd!$ elements, each quotient has dimension at most $\ell^dd!$ over a field. The specialisations $f(t)=\prod_i(t-q_H^i)^{\lambda_i}$ and $f(t)=\prod_i(t-i)^{\lambda_i}$ are instances of the two branches with $\ell=\sum_i\lambda_i$. For $\ell=0$ the imposed relation is $1=0$, giving the zero algebra for $d>0$ and $A$ for $d=0$, as stated. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

items.title: Degenerate affine Hecke ordered monomials form a basis
items.statement:
Let $F$ be any field and let $H_d^{\deg}$ be the algebra generated by commuting
$x_1,\dots,x_d$ and symmetric-group generators $s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ with
$$s_rx_r=x_{r+1}s_r-1,\qquad s_rx_{r+1}=x_rs_r+1,\qquad s_rx_j=x_js_r\quad(j\notin\{r,r+1\}),$$
together with the symmetric-group quadratic, braid and distant commutation
relations, as in the degenerate clause of
[[def-type-a-affine-presentations-and-charged-cyclotomic-quotients]]
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]],
[[thm-the-symmetric-group-has-the-coxeter-presentation]]). Then
$$\{x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_d^{a_d}w:a_j\ge0,\ w\in S_d\}$$
is an $F$-basis of $H_d^{\deg}$. No cyclotomic basis or Brundan–Kleshchev
isomorphism is assumed. For $d=0$ the basis is the singleton empty monomial.

items.title: Nonzero-form cellular heads, cell purity and shared-factor linkage
items.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional cellular algebra over a field $F$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) with cell modules
$C_\lambda$ and cell-form quotients $D_\lambda=C_\lambda/R_\lambda$. Then:

1. every nonzero $D_\lambda$ is an absolutely simple head, all simple
   $A$-modules occur exactly once this way, and $[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\ne0$ implies
   $\lambda\ge\mu$, with $[C_\mu:D_\mu]=1$ whenever $D_\mu\ne0$; here
   "nonzero quotient" means nonzero form, not necessarily a nondegenerate form
   on $C_\lambda$;
2. every nonzero cell module, including labels with zero-form quotient, has
   all its composition factors in a single block
   ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]);
3. two nonzero cell modules share a block exactly when they are linked by a
   finite chain of nonzero cell modules whose neighbouring terms share a
   simple composition factor;
4. for one primitive idempotent $e_\mu$ per simple,
   $$\dim_Fe_\mu Ae_\nu=\sum_\lambda[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\,[C_\lambda:D_\nu].$$

If the cellular index set $T(\lambda)$ is empty, then $C_\lambda=D_\lambda=0$.
Its block support, the set of primitive central idempotents $b$ with
$C_\lambda b\ne0$, is empty, and it has no simple composition factors.
It does not participate in the nonzero-cell linkage criterion of (3), and
its term in the corner sum of (4) is zero.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The cellular data of [F1]–[F4] and the cell modules $C_\lambda$ with

their forms.

1.1 The cell-form scalar and its symmetry. For basis elements $c^\lambda_{us},c^\lambda_{tv}$ the product $c^\lambda_{us}c^\lambda_{tv}$ equals a scalar $G_\lambda(s,t)$ times $c^\lambda_{uv}$ modulo $A^{>\lambda}$ with $G_\lambda(s,t)$ independent of $u,v$: the right cell axiom fixes the first index and the left cell axiom fixes the last one, and comparing the two evaluations leaves the same scalar. The cellular involution gives $G_\lambda(s,t)=G_\lambda(t,s)$. Associativity of the threefold product yields $\langle xa,y\rangle=\langle x,ya^*\rangle$, since both sides compute the coefficient in the cell layer of the same product. [F1, algebra]

1.2 Cell purity and the zero cell. If $T(\lambda)$ is empty, then $C_\lambda=0$, its Gram matrix and form quotient are zero, and every central block projection acts with zero image; thus its block support is empty and it has no simple factors. The corresponding cell layer $J_\lambda$ is zero as well. Now assume $C_\lambda\ne0$ and let $z$ be a central idempotent of $A$. On the cell layer $J_\lambda\cong C_\lambda^{\mathrm{left}}\otimes_FC_\lambda$ the equality of left and right multiplication by $z$ gives $B\otimes\operatorname{Id}=\operatorname{Id}\otimes A_\lambda$ for the first- and second-factor coefficient matrices; comparing matrix coefficients shows every off-diagonal entry of $B$ and $A_\lambda$ vanishes and all diagonal entries of $B$ and $A_\lambda$ are equal, so both are a single scalar $\theta_\lambda$ times the identity. Since $z$ is idempotent, $\theta_\lambda\in\{0,1\}$. Applying this to all primitive central idempotents, whose sum is $1$, exactly one acts as $1$ on the nonzero cell module $C_\lambda$ and the others as $0$; hence $C_\lambda$, and therefore every composition factor of it, lies in one block. This covers labels with zero-form quotient because the tensor argument never divides by the Gram matrix. [F1, F4, algebra]

2.1 Nonzero form gives a simple head. Let $R_\lambda:=\{x\in C_\lambda:\langle x,C_\lambda\rangle=0\}$ be the radical of the form. By step 1.1 the rank-one action is $xc^\lambda_{uv}=\langle x,c^\lambda_u\rangle c^\lambda_v$, which shows that $R_\lambda$ is a submodule and that every vector $x\notin R_\lambda$ generates $C_\lambda$: if $\langle x,c^\lambda_u\rangle\ne0$, then scaling $xc^\lambda_{uv}$ by the inverse scalar produces $c^\lambda_v$ for every $v$. Hence every proper submodule is contained in $R_\lambda$ and $D_\lambda=C_\lambda/R_\lambda$ is simple when the form is nonzero; the criterion is nonzero form, and a degenerate but nonzero form is allowed. Extending scalars preserves the Gram rank and the rank-one action, so $D_\lambda$ is absolutely simple. [F1, step 1.1]

3.1 Every simple occurs. Let $D$ be a simple $A$-module, and choose a cell ideal $I_\lambda$ acting nontrivially on $D$, maximal among such ideals in the finite cell order; then $A^{>\lambda}$ annihilates $D$, while $J_\lambda=I_\lambda/A^{>\lambda}$ does not, so $DJ_\lambda=D$. If the Gram matrix of $C_\lambda$ were zero, the cell-layer multiplication would satisfy $J_\lambda^2=0$ and $DJ_\lambda^2=0$, a contradiction; hence the form is nonzero. Choose $s,u$ and $d\in D$ with $dc^\lambda_{su}\ne0$; the map $c^\lambda_v\mapsto dc^\lambda_{sv}$ has nonzero image, which is all of $D$ by simplicity and factors through the nonzero head $D_\lambda$ of step 2.1, so $D\cong D_\lambda$. This exhausts the simple labels without classifying which multipartitions have nonzero forms. [F1, step 2.1]

3.2 Order and multiplicity. If $\lambda$ does not dominate $\mu$, then $C_\lambda$ annihilates $I_\mu$: products in $I_\lambda\cap I_\mu$ involve only shapes strictly above $\lambda$. Since $D_\mu$ does not annihilate $I_\mu$ by the rank-one action, $[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\ne0$ forces $\lambda\ge\mu$. The radical $R_\lambda$ annihilates $I_\lambda$, while $D_\lambda$ does not, so $[C_\lambda:D_\lambda]=1$ when $D_\lambda\ne0$. Two distinct nonzero heads are not isomorphic: their ideal supports would force $\lambda\ge\mu$ and $\mu\ge\lambda$ simultaneously. [F1, step 2.1]

4.1 The corner identity. Choose one primitive idempotent $e_\mu$ for each simple $D_\mu$ with $\dim D_\nu e_\mu=\delta_{\mu\nu}$. The exact functor $V\mapsto Ve_\mu$ (lift a vector along a surjection and multiply by $e_\mu$; restrict along an injection) gives $\dim C_\lambda e_\mu=[C_\lambda:D_\mu]$. The nonzero heads are self-dual under the involution by the symmetric associative nondegenerate quotient form of steps 1.1 and 2.1, so the corresponding left factor has the same multiplicities. Filtering $A$ by a linear extension of the cellular ideals and applying the two exact projections $e_\mu(-)e_\nu$ to the cell layers $J_\lambda\cong C_\lambda^{\mathrm{left}}\otimes C_\lambda$, dimension additivity gives $\dim_Fe_\mu Ae_\nu=\sum_\lambda[C_\lambda:D_\mu][C_\lambda:D_\nu].$ An empty cell layer contributes zero to both the filtration dimension and every product of its composition multiplicities. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 Blocks and linkage. A finite split algebra has blocks equal to the connected components of the graph on its primitive idempotents with an edge $e$–$f$ whenever $eAf\ne0$ or $fAe\ne0$: a sum of full primitive idempotents over a union of components is central, and conversely a central idempotent cannot separate a nonzero corner, while repeated primitive idempotents of the same simple are linked through the matrix units of $A/\operatorname{rad}A$. By step 4.1 two simple labels have a nonzero corner exactly when they occur together as factors of some cell module, so two simples share a block exactly when a chain of cell modules links their factors. Since by step 1.2 every nonzero cell module is pure and by step 3.1 every simple occurs in a nonzero-form head, two nonzero cell modules lie in the same block exactly when there is a finite chain of nonzero cell modules each neighbouring pair of which shares a simple composition factor. Each nonzero cell has a simple composition factor because it has positive finite dimension. A zero cell has no such factor and has empty block support by step 1.2, so it is absent from this support graph and cannot create a chain edge or a common supported block. [F2, F4, step 1.2, step 4.1]

6.1 Conclusion. Steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1 and 3.2 prove the head, exhaustion, order and multiplicity statement (1); step 1.2 proves cell purity (2); step 4.1 proves the corner identity (4); and step 5.1 proves the exact shared-factor linkage criterion (3). All arguments work over every field and allow degenerate nonzero cell forms, nonzero cells with zero-form quotient, and empty index sets with zero cell modules and empty block support. [step 3.2, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

items.title: Selfadjoint weight Gram valuations detect Jantzen classes
items.statement:
In Leaf A suppose 1=sum_nu e_nu is a finite decomposition into pairwise orthogonal idempotents of A, with e_nu*=e_nu. Write M_nu=e_nu M and G_nu for the restricted Gram matrix. Then each M_nu is finite free, each restricted generic form is nondegenerate, and

$$\sum_{s>0}\dim_F e_\nu M_F^s=\nu_\pi(\det G_\nu).$$

For a split finite-dimensional highest-weight algebra S_F whose standard classes [Delta(mu)] form a Z-basis of K0, if the matrix K_{mu nu}=dim e_nu Delta(mu) has a square unitriangular submatrix indexed by partition weights, then the weight-character map ch:K0 -> Z^{weights}, [N] -> (dim e_nu N)_nu is injective. It follows that a class equality involving Jantzen pieces is equivalent to the corresponding equalities of weight Gram valuations.
items.strategy:
**Statement.** In Leaf A suppose 1=sum_nu e_nu is a finite decomposition into pairwise orthogonal idempotents of A, with e_nu*=e_nu. Write M_nu=e_nu M and G_nu for the restricted Gram matrix. Then each M_nu is finite free, each restricted generic form is nondegenerate, and

$$\sum_{s>0}\dim_F e_\nu M_F^s=\nu_\pi(\det G_\nu).$$

For a split finite-dimensional highest-weight algebra S_F whose standard classes [Delta(mu)] form a Z-basis of K0, if the matrix K_{mu nu}=dim e_nu Delta(mu) has a square unitriangular submatrix indexed by partition weights, then the weight-character map ch:K0 -> Z^{weights}, [N] -> (dim e_nu N)_nu is injective. It follows that a class equality involving Jantzen pieces is equivalent to the corresponding equalities of weight Gram valuations.

**Proof.** The decomposition M=sum e_nu M is direct, and each summand is a direct summand of a finite free O-module, hence free: choose generators, use the preceding DVR elimination on the inclusion, or the fact that a submodule of a finite free module over the DVR is free. For nu!=rho, b(e_nu x,e_rho y)=b(x,e_nu e_rho y)=0. A vector in M_nu,K orthogonal to its summand is orthogonal to all summands and is zero by generic nondegeneracy. Thus the restricted form is nondegenerate. Orthogonality gives M(s)=direct sum M_nu(s), and reduction respects this direct sum. Leaf A applied to M_nu proves the displayed equality.

Each functor N -> e_nu N is exact: injectivity and kernels follow by restriction, and a lift of y=e_nu y in a quotient can be replaced by e_nu x. Thus ch is additive and defined on K0. Write an element as sum_mu a_mu[Delta(mu)]. Its coordinates on the partition weights are the integer row vector a multiplied by a unitriangular matrix K. This matrix is invertible over Z by finite triangular elimination. If the character is zero, a=0. Apply this injectivity to sum_s [Delta(lambda)^s] - sum_mu J_{lambda mu}[Delta(mu)] and use the valuation equality just proved. No Schur functor, residue-sequence character, rationalization, or semisimple Hecke Grothendieck group is used.

items.title: Symmetric polynomial centers have primitive split content idempotents
items.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional unital algebra over a field $F$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]), with commuting elements
$x_1,\dots,x_d$ and split joint regular-module generalized-eigenprojectors
$p_{\mathrm{word}}\in A$: the $p_{\mathrm{word}}$ are pairwise orthogonal,
sum to $1$, and $(x_r-\mathrm{word}_r)p_{\mathrm{word}}$ is nilpotent for every
$r$. For each finite multiset $\alpha$ of eigenvalues let
$e_\alpha:=\sum_{\mathrm{word}\ \text{of multiset}\ \alpha}p_{\mathrm{word}}$,
and assume each $e_\alpha$ is central. If $Z(A)$ is the image of the symmetric
polynomial ring in $x_1,\dots,x_d$
([[def-symmetric-polynomial]], [[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]),
then each $e_\alpha$ is zero or primitive central, and its nonzero terms are
exactly all primitive central idempotents of $A$
([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]).
No splitting-simple-module hypothesis and no algebraic-closure hypothesis on
$F$ is required. For $d=0$ the asserted symmetric-center hypothesis says
$Z(A)=F\cdot1$ and yields the same conclusion.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The data of the Statement and [F1]–[F3]. If $d=0$ there is nothing

to prove beyond $Z(A)=F\cdot1$, whose only idempotents are $0$ and $1$; assume

$d\ge1$ and fix a content $\alpha$ with $e:=e_\alpha\ne0$.

1.1 The nilpotent ideal of the content summand. For $1\le k\le d$ let $a_k$ be the value of $\sigma_k$ on any word of content $\alpha$ (independent of the order of the word). On the summand $p_{\mathrm{word}}A$ inside $eA$ write $x_r=\mathrm{word}_r+N_r$ with commuting nilpotents $N_r$ by [F1]. Choose $M$ with $N_r^M=0$ for all $r$; then every product of more than $d(M-1)$ monomials of positive degree in the $N_r$ vanishes, because among more than $d(M-1)$ factors some $N_r$ occurs at least $M$ times (finite pigeonhole). Hence every polynomial in the $N_r$ with zero constant term is nilpotent, and in particular $N_k:=e\sigma_k(x)-a_ke$ is nilpotent on every $p_{\mathrm{word}}A$; since there are finitely many words, a common exponent makes $N_k$ nilpotent in $eA$. The $N_k$ commute, and the ideal $J$ they generate in the commutative ring $eZ(A)$ is nilpotent by the same degree count. [F1, algebra]

2.1 The center of the content summand is a local ring. By [F2] every symmetric polynomial is a polynomial in $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_d$ (the characteristic-free lexicographic reduction), so the symmetric-center hypothesis gives $eZ(A)=Fe+J .$ Since $e\ne0$ and $J$ is nilpotent, $Fe\cap J=0$: a nonzero element of the intersection is a scalar multiple of $e$ lying in every power of $J$, hence is $0$. Therefore $eZ(A)/J\cong F$, a field, and by [F3] every idempotent of $eZ(A)$ is $0$ or $e$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The nonzero content idempotents are exactly the primitive central idempotents. Step 2.1 shows that each $e_\alpha\ne0$ is a primitive idempotent of $Z(A)$, hence primitive central in $A$. Conversely, let $b$ be a primitive central idempotent of $A$. The $e_\alpha$ are central, pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$, so $b=\sum_\alpha be_\alpha$; if two terms $be_\alpha$ were nonzero, they would be orthogonal nonzero idempotents summing to the primitive idempotent $b$, a contradiction, so exactly one term equals $b$, namely the $e_\alpha$ with $be_\alpha\ne0$. Hence the nonzero $e_\alpha$ are precisely the primitive central idempotents, and the blocks of $A$ are exactly the nonzero content summands. No algebraic closure, splitting-simple-module theorem, power-sum generation, division by $d!$, or level-one restriction is used. [F1, step 2.1] ∎

items.title: Polynomial spectra and central content sectors of finite cyclotomic Hecke algebras
items.statement:
Use the charged finite-$e$ **field** specialization of
[[def-type-a-affine-presentations-and-charged-cyclotomic-quotients]] over any
field $F$. Then $H^\Lambda_d$ is finite-dimensional before any basis
independence argument. Every polynomial generator has a monic annihilator
split over the residue values $c_i$ ($c_i=q_H^i$ in the nondegenerate branch,
$c_i=i\cdot1_F$ in the degenerate branch
([[lem-cyclotomic-hecke-bounded-ordered-monomials-span]])). The canonical
finite CRT projectors $\varepsilon_r(i)$ and
$e(\nu)=\prod_r\varepsilon_r(\nu_r)$ are orthogonal, sum to $1$, and project
every finite $H$-module onto its joint generalized residue spaces. For each
$\alpha=\sum_in_i\alpha_i$ of height $d$,
$e_\alpha=\sum_{\nu\ \text{of content}\ \alpha}e(\nu)$ is central, and $H$ is
the direct sum of its central ideals $e_\alpha H$, possibly zero; no
primitivity is asserted here. On $e(\nu)$, $z_r-c_{\nu_r}$ is nilpotent, so
all invertible-constant local power series have finite evaluations.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The charged specialization, its cyclotomic quotient $H=H^\Lambda_d$,

and the data of [F1]–[F4]; write $q=q_H$ for the nondegenerate parameter.

1.1 Normal spanning in the affine algebra. In the degenerate branch the mixed relation $s_rp=(s_rp)s_r-(p-s_rp)(x_r-x_{r+1})^{-1}$ moves every polynomial past a simple reflection at the cost of its permuted term and a polynomial lower term; in the nondegenerate branch the relations $X_rT_r=T_rX_{r+1}+(1-q)X_{r+1}$ and $X_{r+1}T_r=T_rX_r+(q-1)X_{r+1}$, together with their inverse-variable forms, move every Laurent variable to the left. Each correction lowers the number of misplaced variable/crossing pairs, so the process terminates; the $T$-words reduce to the finitely many standard words $T_w$ by the Hecke relations, and in the degenerate branch the $s$-words reduce to the permutations $w$. Hence the affine algebra is spanned by the ordered monomials $X^aT_w$ ($a\in\mathbb Z^d$, $w\in S_d$) in the nondegenerate branch and by $x^aw$ ($a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^d$) in the degenerate branch. No independence and no injection of the finite Hecke algebra is assumed. [F1, algebra]

1.2 Global intertwiners. For neighboring polynomial variables $x,y$ the degenerate element $\theta:=s(x-y)+1$ satisfies $\theta x=y\theta$ and $\theta^2=1-(x-y)^2$; the nondegenerate element $\Theta:=T(1-xy^{-1})+1-q$ satisfies $\Theta x=y\Theta$ and $\Theta^2=(x-qy)(y-qx)/(xy)$. Both are identities in the whole affine algebra: substituting the mixed relations and the quadratic relation (using $T^{-1}=q^{-1}T+q^{-1}-1$ in the nondegenerate case) and clearing the nonzero factors gives exactly the displayed products. Hence they remain valid in the cyclotomic quotient. These are the source's global identities for the two branches, proved here by substitution rather than imported. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Monic propagation. Suppose the split monic polynomial $f$ of degree $D$ annihilates the old variable $x$. Multiplying the corresponding identity of step 1.2 by $f(x)$ and using $f(x)=0$ gives $f(y)\,\theta^2=0\quad\text{or}\quad f(y)\,\Theta^2=0,$ i.e. $f(y)r(x,y)=0$ with $r$ the respective quadratic in $x,y$ (in the nondegenerate case after multiplying by the commuting unit $xy$). Let $C:=F[z]/(f(z))$ with power basis $1,z,\dots,z^{D-1}$ and consider multiplication by $r(z,y)$ on $C[y]$. Its matrix $M(y)$ has leading coefficient $-\operatorname{Id}$ in the degenerate case and $-q\operatorname{Id}$ in the nondegenerate case; hence $\det M(y)$ has invertible leading coefficient. The adjugate identity [F3], applied to the basis vector $1$, gives $r(z,y)\operatorname{adj}(M(y))=\det M(y)$; lifting this identity from $C[y]$ back to $F[z,y]$ and using the defining relation of $C$, then multiplying by $f(y)$ and using $f(y)r(x,y)=0$, yields $f(y)\det M(y)=0$. Dividing by the invertible leading scalar produces a monic annihilator of the next variable. No flatness, algebraic closure, generic faithfulness or denominator difference is used. [F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Spectral inclusion. If $f(z)=\prod_a(z-a)^{m_a}$ is split with roots $a$, the same power-basis determinant factors as $\prod_ar(a,y)$ with the multiplicities $m_a$: the multiplication matrix is triangular after decomposing $C$ into the finite factors $(z-a)^{m_a}$ (or by the companion-matrix resultant identity). In the degenerate branch the new roots are $a+1,a-1$, and in the nondegenerate branch they are $qa,q^{-1}a$. Starting from $\prod_i(x_1-i)^{\lambda_i}$ therefore produces only roots in the prime-field residue set $\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ (closed under $a\mapsto a\pm1$), and starting from $\prod_i(X_1-q^i)^{\lambda_i}$ produces only roots in $\{q^i:i\in I\}$ (closed under $a\mapsto q^{\pm1}a$). Multiplicities are retained and no square-free assumption is made; in the nondegenerate branch all roots are nonzero, so every annihilator has nonzero constant coefficient and expresses the inverse variable as a polynomial in that variable. [step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Finiteness. Applying step 2.1 successively along the positions shows that every polynomial generator has a finite-degree monic annihilator; its monic relation bounds the exponents of that generator, and in the nondegenerate branch it also eliminates negative exponents. The bounded normal spanning of [F2], together with the normal spanning of step 1.1, therefore expresses every element of the quotient through finitely many exponent tuples and the finitely many $T_w$ (respectively $w$). Hence $H$ is finite-dimensional over $F$, without using the exact $\ell^dd!$ basis theorem or any independence of the bounded monomials. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Canonical CRT projectors. The minimal polynomial of each polynomial generator on its regular module divides the monic split annihilator constructed in steps 2.1 and 3.1, so it is split with only the required residues $c_i$ as roots. For each position $r$ the pairwise comaximal ideals $\bigl((z_r-c_i)^{m_{r,i}}\bigr)_i$ give, by the finite polynomial division algorithm and the Chinese remainder theorem [F4], canonical orthogonal projectors $\varepsilon_r(i)$ in the finite-dimensional algebra generated by $z_r$; these project every finite module onto its generalized $c_i$-eigenspace, including the case of a zero factor. Their commuting products $e(\nu)=\prod_r\varepsilon_r(\nu_r)$ are orthogonal and sum to $1$, and act as the simultaneous generalized residue projectors. On the summand $e(\nu)$ the element $z_r-c_{\nu_r}$ is nilpotent by construction, so every power series with invertible constant term has a finite evaluation there. [F3, F4, step 3.2]

5.1 Centrality of the content sectors. Using the Hecke cross and intertwiner identities of step 1.2, the only possible weights of the image of an element supported on a joint generalized residue $\nu$ under a neighboring Hecke generator are $\nu$ and $s_r\nu$; a fixed-content sum $e_\alpha=\sum_{\nu\ \text{of content}\ \alpha}e(\nu)$ is therefore invariant under every generator, hence central. The central idempotents $e_\alpha$ are orthogonal and sum to $1$, so $H$ is the direct sum of its central ideals $e_\alpha H$, some of which may be zero. Primitivity of the $e_\alpha$ is not asserted or inferred from this argument. [F1, step 1.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Conclusion. Steps 1.1 and 3.2 give finite-dimensionality before any basis independence; steps 2.1 and 3.1 give the monic split annihilators with the stated residue values; step 4.1 gives the canonical orthogonal CRT projectors and the nilpotence of $z_r-c_{\nu_r}$ on $e(\nu)$; and step 5.1 gives centrality of the content sectors $e_\alpha$ with $H=\bigoplus_\alpha e_\alpha H$. No primitivity, blockwise BK isomorphism, cyclotomic exact-dimension theorem or global-basis claim is used. [step 3.2, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

items.title: Central content sectors of the cyclotomic Hecke algebra
items.statement:
Work in the charged finite-$e$ specialization of
[[def-type-a-affine-presentations-and-charged-cyclotomic-quotients]] at a
dominant weight $\Lambda$ and rank $d$, and let $H=H^\Lambda_d$. For the
canonical CRT projectors supplied by
[[lem-cyclotomic-hecke-polynomial-spectra-and-central-content-sectors]],
denote by $e(\nu)$ the joint residue projector attached to the residue tuple
$\nu$ and by
$$e_\alpha:=\sum_{\nu\ \text{of content}\ \alpha}e(\nu)$$
their sum at content $\alpha$ ([[def-type-a-affine-presentations-and-charged-cyclotomic-quotients]]).

**Content sector.** Put
$$H^\Lambda_\alpha:=e_\alpha H^\Lambda_d=e_\alpha H^\Lambda_d\,e_\alpha,$$
an ideal and unital algebra with unit $e_\alpha$, called the **central content
sector** of content $\alpha$; it may be the zero algebra, and at this stage it
is NOT asserted to be a primitive block. The two descriptions coincide because
$e_\alpha$ is a central idempotent.

**Named nilpotent generators.** On $H^\Lambda_\alpha$ put
$$y_r:=\sum_\nu(x_r-\nu_r)\,e(\nu)\quad\text{(degenerate branch)},\qquad y_r:=\sum_\nu\bigl(1-q_H^{-\nu_r}X_r\bigr)e(\nu)\quad\text{(nondegenerate branch)}.$$
By the spectral supplier these named elements are commuting nilpotents on the
sector, and they provide the local variables in which the sector is compared
with the corresponding KLR block.

**Boundary conventions.** For $\alpha=0$ one has $e_{\mathrm{empty}}=1$ and
$H^\Lambda_0=F$ at rank zero. Later primitivity statements may identify the
nonzero sectors with the blocks of $H$, but that identification does not
change the objects named here. This definition introduces no new primitivity
or basis assertion of its own and uses no choice principle.
items.strategy: These are names for already proved finite CRT/projector and central-corner objects; the Definition introduces no new primitivity or basis assertion.

items.title: Charged core height matrices: content-preserving descent and minimal switch connectivity
items.statement:
Fix finite $e\ge2$, $\ell\ge1$ and integer charges $c_1,\dots,c_\ell$. Give the
nodes of component $a$ the residue $c_a+j-i\pmod e$. Write $C_i$ for the
residue counts, $\delta_i$ for removable minus addable $i$-nodes, and
$m_i:=\#\{a:c_a\equiv i\}$. Then
$$\delta_i=2C_i-C_{i-1}-C_{i+1}-m_i,$$
with both neighbouring terms retained (and counted twice) at $e=2$. Equal hubs
and equal size are together equivalent to equal content. For componentwise
$e$-cores let $b_{ia}$ be the largest charged beta bead on runner $i$ and
$$t_{ia}:=\frac{b_{ia}-i}{e} .$$
Cores of fixed hub and charges correspond exactly to integer matrices with
fixed row sums and column sums $c_a-e$; for two such cores the size difference
is $\frac e2$ times the difference of $\sum t_{ia}^2$. Every nonminimum-size
core admits a finite same-hub core-switch path that never increases size and
ends at strictly smaller size, and every pair of minimum-size cores is
connected by equal-size switches. A switch subtracts $1$ at $(i,a),(j,b)$ and
adds $1$ at $(i,b),(j,a)$; each path switch can be oriented with
$\gamma=t_{ia}-t_{ib}-t_{ja}+t_{jb}\ge2$, giving size change $-e(\gamma-2)$.
Minimum cores exist for every nonempty fixed-hub class.
items.strategy:
**Given:** the charged beta/core conventions and [[lem-ultra-tight-multisets-admit-column-potentials]].

Fix e≥2, ℓ≥1 and integer charges c₁,…,cℓ. A component λ^(a) has beta set Bₐ={λ_i^(a)+cₐ−i:i≥1}. It contains all sufficiently negative integers and no sufficiently positive integers, and for large N it has N+cₐ elements ≥−N. Conversely every such set gives a partition: order its elements β₁>β₂>⋯ and put λ_i=β_i−cₐ+i. These integers are decreasing, eventually zero, and therefore nonnegative.

A bead move u→u−h, where u∈B and u−h∉B, unwraps a rim hook of length h with foot residue u−h+1 modulo e. This can be checked directly: if β_i=u and β_j<u−h<β_(j−1), the rows i through j−1 change by the shifted boundary between those two beta positions; the lost border strip has h boxes. Its lowest row is j−1 and its leftmost lost column there is (u−h)−cₐ+j, so its foot content is u−h+1. Reversing the move wraps the hook with foot residue its starting beta position plus one. In particular moving a bead upward one position on its runner removes an e-hook. Repeating packs every runner upwards. The result is independent of removal order because the number of beads relative to the negative reference tail on each runner is preserved. The packed component is its e-core. Every e-hook contains one node of each residue, so hook removal leaves the hub invariant and subtracts the all-one vector from the residue counts.

Let Cᵢ(λ) be node residue counts and mᵢ=#{a:cₐ≡i mod e}. Set δᵢ=number of removable i-nodes minus number of addable i-nodes. We have

δᵢ=2Cᵢ−Cᵢ₋₁−Cᵢ₊₁−mᵢ, with cyclic indices (the two neighboring terms coincide and occur twice if e=2).

One direct proof is induction while adjoining nodes: the empty multipartition has δᵢ=−mᵢ; adjoining a node of residue j changes the boundary count by +2 at j and −1 at each of j−1,j+1, counted twice when e=2. These changes follow by recording the occupied/vacant beta positions before and after the one-position bead move; all other adjacent occupancies cancel. The residue-count expression changes in exactly the same way. This also derives Fayers weight-paper Lemmas 2.3 and 3.1 without a Lie-theoretic assumption.

If two multipartitions have equal hubs, their residue-count difference d satisfies 2dᵢ−dᵢ₋₁−dᵢ₊₁=0. Thus the first differences dᵢ−dᵢ₋₁ are all equal; summing them around the cycle makes this common difference zero. Therefore d is constant. Consequently equal hub and equal size imply equal content; equal hubs imply sizes congruent modulo e.

For a component core let bᵢₐ be the largest bead on runner i, 0≤i<e, and define the integer

tᵢₐ=(bᵢₐ−i)/e.

The packed beta set on runner i is {i+ek:k≤tᵢₐ}. The column sums satisfy Σᵢtᵢₐ=cₐ−e, by counting beads ≥−eL for large L. Writing Rᵢ=Σₐtᵢₐ, the hub satisfies δᵢ=Rᵢ−Rᵢ₋₁ for 1≤i<e and δ₀=R₀−R_(e−1)−ℓ. Since ΣᵢRᵢ=Σₐcₐ−eℓ is fixed, equal hub is equivalent to equal row sums. Thus cores of a fixed hub and charges are exactly integer e×ℓ matrices with fixed row and column sums.

If κ,η are such cores, then

|η|−|κ|=(e/2)(Σᵢₐtᵢₐ(η)²−Σᵢₐtᵢₐ(κ)²).

To prove it, count beta numbers ≥−eL in each component. Their number is eL+cₐ, the same for both cores. Their sum changes by Σᵢ i Δtᵢₐ+(e/2)ΣᵢΔ(tᵢₐ²+tᵢₐ). From β_j=λ_j+cₐ−j, the change in this sum equals the change in partition size. Sum over a: equal row sums kill Σᵢ iΣₐΔtᵢₐ, and equal margins kill the linear ΣΔt term. This proves the formula. In particular the squared-norm difference is even, so the displayed expression is an integer multiple of e.

Use the column-potential lemma just cited in the following finite energy argument.

Let T=(tᵢₐ) be an integer e×ℓ matrix with fixed margins. A switch in distinct rows i,j and distinct columns a,b replaces

(tᵢₐ,tᵢ_b,tⱼₐ,tⱼ_b) by (tᵢₐ−1,tᵢ_b+1,tⱼₐ+1,tⱼ_b−1).

Put γ=tᵢₐ−tᵢ_b−tⱼₐ+tⱼ_b. Its squared-norm change is 4−2γ. Hence γ=2 is a zero-energy switch and γ≥3 strictly decreases energy. Regard the e labeled rows of T as a multiset in L_ℓ. They are tight exactly when every γ≤2; switches with γ=2 are exactly zero exchanges.

If the row multiset is not ultra-tight, a finite sequence of zero switches leads to a non-tight matrix. There γ≥3 for some rows and columns, giving a strict descent. Every intermediate matrix has the same margins, and the descent lowers core size by e(γ−2), while zero switches preserve it.

If it is ultra-tight, the lemma provides a column potential sₐ such that each row of U=(tᵢₐ−sₐ) has maximum minus minimum at most one. For a fixed integer row sum, such a row minimizes the sum of squares over all integer rows: if entries differ by ≥2, transferring one from the larger to the smaller lowers the square sum by at least two; repeated transfers terminate. Its minimum is achieved exactly by rows whose entries differ by at most one. Column potentials do not affect comparisons of total squared norm between matrices with the same column sums, since

Σ(tᵢₐ−sₐ)²=Σtᵢₐ²−2ΣₐsₐΣᵢtᵢₐ+eΣₐsₐ².

Thus T is a global minimum among matrices of its margins. Conversely a global minimum cannot admit a strict descent after zero switches, so its row multiset is ultra-tight. Starting from any T, repeated zero-path/strict-descent steps reach a global minimum: all matrices represent genuine cores of nonnegative integer size, and strict descent lowers that size by at least e.

Now let T,V be two global minima of the same margins. Use the column potential s of T. Every row of U=T−s is balanced, say its entries are uᵢ or uᵢ+1. Since V−s has the same row sums and the same total energy, each of its rows also attains the row minimum and therefore has entries uᵢ or uᵢ+1. Subtract uᵢ from row i. We obtain two binary e×ℓ matrices A,B with identical row and column sums.

Here is a complete binary-switch connectivity proof (Fayers Proposition 2.4, author PDF pp.15–16). If A≠B, write D=A−B. Its nonzero entries are ±1, with all row and column sums zero. Starting at a +1, alternate a −1 in its row and a +1 in that column. A repeated location gives an alternating cycle. Choose a shortest such cycle, with distinct rows i₀,…,i_(t−1) and columns j₀,…,j_(t−1), where D_(i_k,j_k)=+1 and D_(i_k,j_(k+1))=−1, cyclically. If t=2, switch its rectangle in A to agree with B there. If t>2 inspect A_(i₀,j_(t−1)) and B_(i₀,j_(t−1)). If A there is 0, switching the rectangle with rows i₀,i_(t−1) and columns j₀,j_(t−1) gives a binary A' and strictly fewer discrepancies with B. If B there is 1, the reverse switch on B gives a binary B' with strictly fewer discrepancies with A. If neither condition holds, D there is +1 and a shorter alternating cycle exists, contradicting minimality. Induct on the discrepancy count; every binary switch preserves margins. Hence A and B are connected by binary switches.

Lifting these binary switches to T gives switches with γ=2 and thus preserves core size and hub. Therefore any two minimum-size cores of a given hub and fixed charges are connected by equal-size elementary core switches. Any nonminimum core admits a core-switch path that preserves hub, never increases size, and ends at strictly smaller size. These are exactly the finite-e descent and reduced-core connectivity facts consumed by the Lyle–Mathas max-weight argument. This proves F locally without Fayers' weight nonnegativity, pairwise-weight formula, or matrix-alignment Proposition 2.5 as additional inputs.

items.title: Cyclic type-A KLR regular Hom norm gives the total dimension
items.statement:
Let $F$ be any field, $I=\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$ with finite $e\ge2$, and use the
standard homogeneous cyclotomic KLR quotient at $\Lambda=\sum_i\lambda_i\Lambda_i$
for the cyclic affine type-A Cartan datum and admissible graded parameters
([[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]],
[[def-cyclotomic-klr-quotient-at-a-dominant-weight]]). Put
$\ell=\sum_i\lambda_i$ and
$$B_d=\bigoplus_{\operatorname{ht}\beta=d}R^\Lambda(\beta).$$
Then $\dim_FB_d=\ell^dd!$ for $d>0$, and $B_0=F$ has dimension one. The proof
uses the basic first induction-restriction adjunction and the mixed relations
on projective $K_0$ modulo $v-1$, where $v$ is the formal grading variable,
independent of any Hecke parameter $q_H$. No Frobenius theorem, tensor-form
perfectness, highest-weight or global-basis isometry, or Hecke basis is
required. If $\ell=0$ and $d>0$, then $B_d=0$.

**Open obligation.** The proof consumes the sibling suppliers
[[thm-cyclotomic-klr-induction-is-projective-on-the-right]] (step 3.1),
[[thm-cyclotomic-klr-sl-two-categorical-commutator]] (step 2.1) and
[[lem-cyclotomic-normalized-functors-give-an-integrable-quantum-action]]
(step 2.1); if any of these is not yet authored, this item's decision stays
escalated until the supplier and the exact use are reconciled.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The cyclic KLR data of [F1]–[F4], the operators

$D=\sum_iF_i^{\mathrm{basic}}$, $E=\sum_iE_i^{\mathrm{basic}}$ on projective

$K_0$ modulo $v-1$, and the classes $P_d=[B_d]$, $P_0=[F]$.

1.1 Rank decomposition. For fixed $d$, the corner idempotents $e(\beta,i)$ over all root components $\beta$ of height $d-1$ and colors $i$ are orthogonal and sum to $1_{B_d}$: each word has exactly one last color and one prefix root, so it lies in exactly one corner. By [F1] the multiplication map $\bigoplus_{\beta,i}B_de(\beta,i)\otimes_{R^\Lambda(\beta)}R^\Lambda(\beta)\to B_d$ is an isomorphism; spelling out the left action by the basic induction functor gives $P_d=DP_{d-1}=D^dP_0$. The zero-corner case gives $B_de(\beta,i)=0$ and is included since its summand is zero. [F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 The mixed commutators at $v=1$. Forgetting the grading shifts in the same-color categorical decomposition gives $[E_i^{\mathrm{basic}},F_i^{\mathrm{basic}}]=h_i(\Lambda-\beta)\operatorname{Id}$ on the root component $\beta$; its positive identity summands contribute $h_i$ copies and its negative identity summands contribute the signed counterpart, so the integral $[h_i]_v$ specializes at $v=1$ to the integer $h_i$ with no division by $v-v^{-1}$. The unequal-color mixed relation gives $[E_i^{\mathrm{basic}},F_j^{\mathrm{basic}}]=0$ for $i\ne j$. Hence $[E,D]=\sum_i[E_i^{\mathrm{basic}},F_i^{\mathrm{basic}}] =\Bigl(\sum_ih_i(\Lambda-\beta)\Bigr)\operatorname{Id}$ on root component $\beta$. For affine type A every Cartan column sums to zero, including the double-edge matrix at $e=2$, so $\sum_ih_i(\Lambda-\beta)=\sum_i\lambda_i-\sum_j\beta_j\sum_ia_{ij}=\ell$ independently of $\beta$. Therefore $[E,D]=\ell\cdot\operatorname{Id}$, and since rank-zero restriction is zero, $EP_0=0$; expanding $[E,D^d]=d\ell D^{d-1}$ gives $EP_d=d\ell\,P_{d-1}$. [F2, algebra]

2.1 The Hom-norm recurrence. For finite graded projectives define $h$ as in [F4]; it is additive in both variables, unchanged by shifts, and descends to projective $K_0$ modulo $v-1$. Pairing distinct root blocks by zero and summing over a fixed rank, the ordinary first adjunction $F_i^{\mathrm{basic}}\dashv E_i^{\mathrm{basic}}$ gives $h(F_i^{\mathrm{basic}}P,Q)=h(P,E_i^{\mathrm{basic}}Q)$, hence $h(DP,Q)=h(P,EQ)$; all restricted modules remain finite projectives by [F3], so the recurrence stays inside the declared group. Combining with step 1.2, $h(P_d,P_d)=h(DP_{d-1},P_d)=h(P_{d-1},EP_d) =d\ell\,h(P_{d-1},P_{d-1}).$ [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Conclusion. The initial value is $h(P_0,P_0)=\dim_F\operatorname{End}_F(F)=1$; since $\operatorname{End}_{B_d}(B_d)\cong B_d^{\mathrm{op}}$ by right multiplication, $h(P_d,P_d)=\dim_FB_d$, and induction on $d$ gives $\dim_FB_d=\ell^dd!$ as an ordinary integer. Nothing reduces the integer dimension or the factor $d\ell$ inside $F$, so the argument covers every field characteristic; for $\ell=0$ and $d>0$ the recurrence gives $\dim_FB_d=0$; and for $d=0$, independently of $\ell$, $B_0=F$ has the singleton empty monomial as basis. No Frobenius theorem, tensor-form perfectness, highest-weight or global-basis isometry, Hecke basis or choice principle is used. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎
